server_side_pipeline_ms.note: Parsed from the runtime's structured logs (span: infer, infer_latency_ns), excluding HTTP transport and JSON encoding. Client round trips above are dominated by sending the encoded image as a JSON number array; the binary tensor extension would close that gap.

caveats: Inference is TensorRT FP16 on GPU in all three configurations and identical between them.
GPU postprocessing uses a custom CUDA DALI operator plugin; the plugin and the serialized pipeline are tied to one DALI version (1.51.2 here).
DALI outputs are copied device->host by the backend and re-uploaded by the next step. Writing straight into the downstream device buffer would remove two full-tensor copies per frame.
transport_note: All figures below use the HTTP binary tensor extension. An earlier run used JSON 'data' arrays, which for a 98 KB encoded image and multi-MB float tensors dominated the measurement: client medians were 303.8 / 276.7 / 244.6 ms for the three configurations versus 155.0 / 164.8 / 74.0 ms here. gRPC was NOT used; this build has NEURIPLO_RUNTIME_ENABLE_GRPC=OFF, and a gRPC comparison remains unmeasured.

stage_decomposition_ms.note: Each model measured in isolation, server-side. Compared against tritonic's published per-stage medians for the same model and GPU.
stage_decomposition_ms.finding: GPU postprocessing compute is identical (2.58 vs 2.59 ms) -- same CUDA plugin. The entire remaining gap is host round-trips: DALI copies its output device->host and the next step re-uploads it. Preprocessing pays 7.6 ms for a 4.9 MB tensor that tritonic never moves off the device.

key_finding: GPU preprocessing alone is now a clear win (78.7 ms vs 123.5 ms for CPU preprocessing), and GPU pre + GPU post is 4.6x the all-CPU path at 26.8 ms. Before the TensorRT raw-output fix, GPU preprocessing alone measured as a net LOSS, which was misread as PCIe transfer cost; it was actually the variant round-trip scaling with tensor element count, which hurt the GPU-preprocessed path most because it moves the largest tensors.

transport_comparison_client_median_ms.note: Same server, same models, three transports. JSON is the outlier; HTTP binary and gRPC agree within ~1.5 ms, which means transport is not the bottleneck once the tensor is not being spelled out as JSON numbers. The remaining time is server-side pipeline work.

outstanding_optimization.title: Device-side tensor handoff between pipeline steps
outstanding_optimization.why: Per-stage measurement puts the whole neuriplo-vs-tritonic gap in host round-trips: GPU postprocess compute is identical (2.58 vs 2.59 ms, same CUDA plugin), while DALI preprocess costs 7.66 ms against 0.03 ms because tritonic's DALI writes straight into the TensorRT input binding and never moves the 4.9 MB tensor off the device.
outstanding_optimization.feasibility: Both halves verified. TRTInfer already cudaMallocs its own buffers_ and binds them with setInputTensorAddress, so an input buffer pointer can be exposed. daliOutputCopy accepts device_type_t::GPU, so DALI can write device-to-device into that pointer. No inline-inference operator exists in DALI 1.51.2, so fusing the whole chain into one pipeline is not an option.
design: InferenceInterface: optional input_device_buffer(index) and copy_output_to_device(index, dst, bytes), defaulting to unsupported so no existing backend changes.
TRTInfer: return buffers_[index]; skip the host-to-device copy for inputs a caller has already filled.
DALIInfer: implement copy_output_to_device via daliOutputCopy with a GPU destination.
Pipeline executor: when a producing step supports device output and the consuming step accepts device input, hand over the pointer instead of host bytes.
outstanding_optimization.expected: Removes ~7.6 ms on the preprocess hop and part of the 5 ms TensorRT delta; the TRT->postprocess hop moves a further 3.3 MB.
outstanding_optimization.risk: A partially-correct device path silently corrupts tensors rather than failing, so it needs per-hop verification against the host path.
outstanding_optimization.status: Deprioritised, not done. The premise -- that the whole gap was host round-trips -- was only half right: removing the per-scalar variant round-trip closed it entirely and put neuriplo at/below tritonic. True device-to-device handoff would still remove ~24MB/frame of PCIe traffic and remains the next lever, but it is now an incremental optimisation against a competitive baseline rather than a gap-closer, and it carries the silent-corruption risk noted below.

trt_raw_output_path_ab.note: A/B on one machine in one session: binaries built from the same tree, differing only in whether TRTInfer overrides get_infer_results_raw(). Client medians over the HTTP binary tensor extension, 30 iterations after 3 warmup, interleaved across the three ensembles.
trt_raw_output_path_ab.change: TRTInfer implements get_infer_results_raw(), copying device output buffers straight into contiguous host bytes. Previously it inherited the default, which routes through get_infer_results() and materialises one 16-byte std::variant per output scalar (~2.6M scalars for yolo26m-seg, ~42MB of variant vector) before re-serialising it.
trt_raw_output_path_ab.correctness: The 50-frame CPU-vs-DALI agreement run reproduced the recorded baseline exactly (701 reference, 739 candidate, 641 matched, 0.9144/0.8674), so the raw path emits identical tensors -- this is a pure overhead removal, not a behaviour change.
trt_raw_output_path_ab.vs_tritonic: tritonic's measured ensemble for the same model and GPU is 27.04 ms. neuriplo's GPU pre+post is now 23.9 ms server-side / 26.8 ms client-observed, so the gap this file previously attributed to host round-trips is closed. Most of it was never PCIe traffic at all -- it was per-scalar variant construction on the host.

known_bug.title: Heap corruption in the GPU-postprocess ensemble, pre-existing
known_bug.severity: Server aborts (SIGABRT). Reproducible, but the aborting allocation varies.
known_bug.repro: Load yolo26seg (tensorrt), yolo_pre and yolo_post (dali), and the three ensembles. Run the HTTP binary-transport benchmark across all three ensembles, then issue a JSON-transport request to yolo26seg_gpu. It aborts on the first such request with 'malloc(): corrupted top size' or 'double free or corruption (!prev)'.
known_bug.not_caused_by: The TensorRT raw-output change. Verified by reproducing it identically on a binary built from the parent commit.
ruled_out: DALI overrunning its output buffer: a 64-byte redzone around every daliOutputCopy destination never trips.
A DALI external input whose declared shape outruns its buffer: checked explicitly before daliSetExternalInput, never trips.
RealNeuriploAdapter::infer, which is where gdb caught the abort -- it resizes and memcpys exactly raw.bytes.size(). It is the first large allocation after the damage, not the writer.
known_bug.evidence: gdb backtrace: abort in _int_malloc for a 564495-byte request from RealNeuriploAdapter::infer on a ModelScheduler thread, in a non-main arena (av=0x7ffef8000030). The corrupting write happened earlier in that arena.
known_bug.next_step: Run the runtime under ASAN with the DALI and TensorRT backends, or set MALLOC_CHECK_=3, to catch the write rather than the detection.
